newsitem.title: CHINA: Mao backed private sector, argues China economist.
newsitem.headline: Mao backed private sector, argues China economist.

text.p: A senior liberal economist on Tuesday joined a heated debate on public ownership, blaming the Soviet Union for China's reliance on a now-flagging state sector and saying even the late Chairman Mao Zedong did not oppose private enterprise.
In an interview with the China Economic Times, Wu Jinglian urged the communist government to encourage restructuring of lumbering state enterprises and to shrink the state-owned sector.

China's long-held socialist creed that state firms should form the dominant sector of the economy was an outdated theory put forward by the Soviet Union, whose own socialist system had collapsed due to its inability to adapt, Wu said.

Leaders and economists are currently debating whether to break with four decades of socialist tradition by moving away from the sacred cow of the state sector as the dominant part of the economy and allow private enterprise a larger role.
Wu was firm that the idea of state dominance was an imported theory and not necessarily applicable in China.

"The theory that only the two systems, those of state ownership and collective ownership under state control, can exist under socialism was created by Stalin during a power struggle at the end of the 1920s," Wu said.
He pulled out two of China's biggest guns to back his case and to attack opponents of greater private ownership.
He quoted the late revolutionary Chairman Mao Zedong as saying: "The management plan of relying on the state for everything violates the concept that the people create history."

Wu did not stop there, but turned to the late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, who nearly two decades ago launched the sweeping market-oriented economic reforms that have undermined public sector dominance.

He cited a string of quotations from Deng's speeches, including one remark in which the reformist leader who swapped Stalinist central planning for capitalist-style stock markets said many "did not have a clear picture" of socialism.
"Facts prove that increasing the proportion of state ownership cannot guarantee the consolidation of socialist society," Wu said.
"Whether a country is socialist is not decided by the proportion of the economy in state hands," he said.

Economists and analysts say that finding the courage to push ahead with unpalatable reform of the flagging and long cosseted state sector will almost certainly be a major issue at a crucial Communist Party congress, held every five years, in late September or early October.
The most heated debate has focused on whether China can remain socialist if it adopts more diverse ownership, allowing the private sector a greater share at the expense of the state.
"We should have a clear understanding," Wu said.

"It was because of their long support of Soviet-style socialist theory that the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe saw ossification of ideas, a slowdown in development, social stagnation, and finally the result was that the Communist Party lost power," he said.
"In comparison to this, China's reforms have taken a completely different route," Wu said, referring to the world's fastest expanding economy with growth of 9.8 percent last year.

However, China has made slow progress in reforming state industry, of which 70 percent is loss-making, amid fears the state would lose its predominance and that bankruptcies and streamlining would result in mass unemployment and social unrest -- anathema to China's communist leadership.
China's lumbering state sector strengthened slightly in the first half to show a net profit after an unprecedented net loss in 1996.
